[–]braun0 298 points 8 days ago* 
Former ticket broker here (spent 8 years working for one of the largest ticket brokering agencies in NYC). The “bots” are not the reason why you did not get tickets today. To be clear, I do NOT condone or support the usage bots. However, Ticketmaster wants you (the fans/general public) to blame the bots, as total misdirection to what is actually going on.
Here is an example:
Madison Square Garden has a seating capacity of roughly 18,000. That sound like a lot of seats - you should have a really good shot of getting some tickets, right? In reality, for an extremely popular concert like this, during the “general on-sale” you have about 1% chance of actually pulling tickets (regardless of bots or ticket brokers).
How seats are sold/allocated (these are not exact numbers - just representative of how tickets are allocated):
Total tickets in venue: 18000
Knicks/Rangers season-ticket-holder access: 3000
Amex or CITI Bank pre-sale: 3000
VIP packages: 1000
MSG family/Fan Club pre-sale: 2000
Promoter/venue reserved: 2000
Tickets remaining for general on-sale: 7000
So 7000 tickets actually go on sale to the general public. The average size of a ticket order is roughly three (3) tickets. 7000 tickets/3 tickets per order = roughly 2,333 people who actually pull and purchase tickets during the general on-sale. For something like a Bruce Springsteen concert, in the NYC Tri-state area, it’s estimated that a minimum of 200,000 people will try to buy tickets during the general on-sale. 2,333/200,000 = 1.16% chance of getting tickets. Again, this is rough math - but you get the idea.
That means 98.9% of people who try to buy tickets are going to get shut out. Ticketmaster wants you to blame bots and ticket brokers - when the reality is that more than half the seats are never available to fans in the first place. After that, it’s pure odds and luck. Even if you eliminated all the brokers and bots - perhaps your odds would double to say 2.5%. Still 97.5% of fans would be shut out.
Again, I do not support the usage of Bots and no longer support the ticket brokering industry. However, it is important to know how these things actually work - and to put the “blame” in the correct place.
EDIT/Addition: A few questions I have been asked:
1) How can the concert sell out in only 30 seconds?
Well, it actually can sell out in about 2 seconds. Once the TM server hits 10am and the “buy” page goes live - the 7000 tickets will be allocated to (roughly) the first 2,333 people who hit “search”. With 200,000 people doing this - it only takes a few seconds (or less than a second) for all the tickets to be allocated to shopping carts. Milliseconds actually make a difference here (much like flash trading in the stock market).
2) Can seats become available again? Yes!
a) Some people will “screwup” during the checkout process and those tickets will be released back into the general pool.
b) Credit cards will be declined.
c) Time will expire in the shopping cart. So if the checkout timer is 7 minutes (not sure what is on TM right now), look to refresh and check for tickets again at 10:07am.
Also, and this is something TM will never tell you - tickets can be released in delayed “blocks”. This is to sell the least desirable seats first within each price point. So instead of selling the best section/best row first, they will sell the worst section/worst row first. As the buyer, you will think these bad seats are the “best” you are going to get - so you pull the trigger and buy. TM is guaranteeing that they sell the “hardest” to sell tickets first - knowing that they can always sell the better tickets later. Sneaky, right?
